title: Cursor: Your AI Pair Programmer
description: Learn Cursor, the AI-first code editor, from install to Agent mode: Tab completion, inline editing, codebase chat, rules, and MCP, all taught step by step for beginners.

lessons.title: Meet Cursor: the editor that reads your mind
lessons.bodyMd:
## A code editor with AI built in, not bolted on

You have probably used AI in a chat window: you describe what you want, it writes some code, you copy it back into your editor, and you fix the parts it got wrong. Cursor flips that around. It is a full code editor, like VS Code, with the AI living inside it. The AI can see your files, suggest code as you type, rewrite selections on command, and even make changes across many files at once.

Cursor is built by a company called Anysphere. It started as a fork of VS Code, the free editor from Microsoft that most developers already use. Because of that, Cursor looks and feels like VS Code: same layout, same file explorer on the left, same terminal at the bottom, same keyboard shortcuts. If you have used VS Code, you already know 90 percent of Cursor. The difference is what happens when you press Tab.

## What "AI-native" actually means

The word you will hear is "AI-native." It means the AI is not a plugin you installed later. It is part of the editor's core. Three things follow from that:

First, the AI sees context automatically. When you ask a question in the chat panel, it already knows which file you have open, what you edited recently, and how your project is structured. You do not have to paste code into a chat box.

Second, the AI can act, not just advise. In Agent mode, Cursor can create files, edit existing ones, run terminal commands, and check its own work. You describe the goal, and it does the typing.

Third, everything is one keystroke away. The features you will use most, Tab completion, inline editing with Cmd+K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux), and the chat panel with Cmd+L (Ctrl+L), are built into the normal rhythm of writing code. You never leave your editor to get help.

## Why developers switched

Cursor became popular fast because it solved an annoyance every developer felt. Writing boilerplate code is boring. Looking up the exact syntax for something you half remember is slow. Explaining your whole project to a chatbot every time you need help is tedious.

Cursor's Tab completion is the headline feature. It does not just finish the current line like older autocomplete. It predicts multi-line edits, entire functions, and sometimes the next several steps of what you are building. Developers report accepting a large share of these suggestions, and the time saved on routine code adds up to close to an hour a day for heavy users.

But the deeper win is codebase awareness. Cursor indexes your project, building a searchable map of it. When you ask "where is the login logic handled," it does not guess. It searches your actual code and answers with real file names and line numbers.

## What this guide will teach you

By the end of this guide you will be able to install Cursor, bring over your VS Code setup, write code with Tab completion, edit with Cmd+K, chat about your codebase, run the Agent on multi-file tasks, write rules that keep the AI consistent, connect external tools with MCP, and understand the privacy and pricing tradeoffs. No prior AI tool experience is assumed. If you can open a file and type, you are ready.

lessons.title: Cursor vs VS Code vs Windsurf: an honest comparison
lessons.bodyMd:
## The three ways to write code with AI in 2026

If you are choosing an AI coding setup, you will run into three names: VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Windsurf. They all do the same job, which is helping you write software faster, but they take different routes. Here is a fair look at each.

## VS Code plus GitHub Copilot

VS Code is the free, open source editor from Microsoft. GitHub Copilot is its AI companion, sold as a subscription. Together they are the most common setup in the world.

The strengths: Copilot is cheap, starting at 10 dollars a month for individuals, with a free tier that includes a monthly allowance of completions and chat messages. It works inside the editor you may already use, and GitHub integration is deep, since the same company owns both. Agent mode exists here too, and it can edit files and run commands.

The tradeoff: Copilot is an extension, not part of the editor's core. Its view of your codebase is shallower than Cursor's. You will spend more effort pointing it at the right files, and multi-file changes need more hand-holding.

## Cursor

Cursor is a standalone editor, a fork of VS Code with AI in its bones. Its Tab completion uses a custom model tuned for predicting your next edit, often several lines at a time. Its chat understands your whole indexed codebase without you pasting anything. Its Agent mode was early and aggressive, and it can plan, edit multiple files, run the terminal, and verify results.

The strengths: the deepest codebase understanding of the three, your choice of frontier models (including Claude, GPT, and Gemini options), and the smoothest VS Code migration, since your extensions, themes, and keybindings import in minutes.

The tradeoffs: it costs 20 dollars a month for Pro, and since 2025 the billing has been credit-based, which confuses people and can push heavy users toward 30 to 50 dollars a month in practice. Privacy needs active attention: your code goes to AI providers for inference by default, and you must turn on Privacy Mode if that matters to you.

## Windsurf

Windsurf, from the company Codeium, is the other AI-first editor. Like Cursor, it is built around an agent that can plan and execute multi-file changes. Its signature idea is "Flows," where the agent and the developer collaborate in a shared loop, and it has a strong reputation for keeping you in control of each step.

The strengths: a generous free tier historically, a polished agent experience, and good performance. Some developers prefer its more deliberate, step-by-step style over Cursor's speed.

The tradeoffs: a smaller ecosystem and community than Cursor, fewer model choices, and like Cursor it is a separate editor you must adopt, not an extension for the one you have.

## Which should you pick

For a beginner learning AI-assisted coding, any of the three will teach you the core skills: prompting well, reviewing AI output, and staying in charge. Cursor is the best-documented and most widely used of the AI-first editors, which is why this guide covers it. The habits you build here, giving good context, writing rules, reviewing diffs, transfer directly to the others.

One honest note: tools converge fast. VS Code keeps adding native AI features, and the gap narrows every year. Pick the tool that fits your budget and workflow today, and invest your real energy in the underlying skills. Those do not expire.

lessons.title: Who Cursor is for (and who should skip it)
lessons.bodyMd:
## The people who get the most from Cursor

Cursor shines for builders. If you are making a side project, a startup MVP, a freelance client site, or learning to code by building real things, Cursor removes the two biggest speed bumps: boilerplate and "how do I even start." You describe what you want, and the editor helps you produce working code in hours instead of days.

It is also excellent for working developers on medium to large codebases. The codebase indexing means you can ask questions like "how does authentication work in this repo" and get answers grounded in your actual files. Refactors that touch a dozen files, the kind of task developers dread, become a single conversation with the Agent.

Freelancers and indie hackers love it because time literally is money. Saving an hour a day on routine code pays for the subscription many times over.

## Who should think twice

Total beginners face a real trap: it is easy to accept AI suggestions without understanding them. If you are learning to program for the first time, Cursor can become a crutch. The fix is simple but requires discipline. Read every suggestion before accepting it, ask the chat to explain code you do not understand, and regularly write small things by hand. Treat Cursor as a mentor, not an autopilot.

Developers on very large monorepos, think hundreds of thousands of lines, report that Cursor can lag and its context gets less reliable. The indexing works best on projects up to a large but normal size.

If you handle highly sensitive code, client work under strict compliance, medical or financial systems, the default data flow may not be acceptable. Your code is sent to AI providers for inference unless you enable Privacy Mode. For some teams that is a dealbreaker, and the enterprise controls cost more.

And if predictable billing matters more than anything, the credit-based pricing can frustrate. Copilot's flat 10 dollars a month is simpler to budget.

## The mindset that makes it work

The developers who love Cursor share one habit: they stay in charge. They review every diff the Agent produces. They run the tests. They ask "why did you do it this way" when something looks odd. The AI is a fast, tireless junior developer. You are the senior engineer who reviews the pull request.

That mindset is the real subject of this guide. The buttons and shortcuts will change over the years. The discipline of directing an AI, verifying its work, and keeping ownership of your codebase will not.

lessons.title: How AI pair programming actually works
lessons.bodyMd:
## From autocomplete to agency: the ladder

AI coding help comes in levels, and Cursor gives you all of them in one place. Understanding the ladder helps you pick the right tool for each moment.

Level one is completion. You type, and the AI suggests the rest. This is Tab completion, and it handles the small stuff: finishing a function signature, filling in a loop, writing the obvious next lines. It is fast, low risk, and you stay fully in control because you approve every suggestion with a keystroke.

Level two is inline editing. You select some code, press Cmd+K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux), and describe the change in plain English: "convert this to async/await" or "add input validation." The AI rewrites just that selection. This is perfect for the tedious transformations that are too small for a chat conversation but annoying to do by hand.

Level three is chat. You ask questions and get explanations, or you ask for code with full context. Chat is read-only by default in the sense that it does not change files until you apply its suggestions, which makes it the safe place to explore and learn.

Level four is the Agent. You give it a goal, like "add a password reset flow," and it plans the work, edits multiple files, runs commands in the terminal, and checks its own results. This is the most powerful level and the one that demands the most supervision.

## The golden rule of context

Here is the single most important idea in this entire guide: the AI is only as good as what it can see. This is called context. If the AI cannot see the relevant files, it will guess, and guesses in code become bugs.

Every Cursor feature is really a context feature. Tab completion sees your open files and recent edits. Chat sees what you attach with @-mentions. The Agent sees your indexed codebase plus whatever rules you wrote. Your job as the human is to be the AI's eyes: point it at the right files, write rules that encode your conventions, and keep your project organized so the index stays useful.

A useful mantra from experienced Cursor users: too little context means hallucination, too much means confusion. Give the AI exactly what it needs for the task at hand, no more and no less.

## Your job description, updated

With Cursor, your job shifts. You write less boilerplate and do more of three things: specifying what you want clearly, reviewing what the AI produced carefully, and testing that it actually works. Specification, review, and verification. That is the new loop.

This feels strange at first, especially if you are used to typing every character yourself. But it is the same shift that happened when compilers, then frameworks, then package managers arrived. Each wave moved developers up a level of abstraction. AI pair programming is the next step up. You are still the builder. You just stopped laying every brick by hand.

lessons.title: Download and install Cursor in ten minutes
lessons.bodyMd:
## Get the installer

Everything starts at cursor.com. The download page detects your operating system automatically and offers the right installer: macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel builds), Windows, or Linux. The download is a few hundred megabytes, roughly the size of VS Code itself, because under the hood that is what it is.

Run the installer like any other application. On macOS, drag Cursor into Applications. On Windows, run the setup executable. On Linux, use the package for your distribution or the portable archive. There is nothing to configure during installation. The interesting choices come after you first launch it.

## Create your account

When Cursor opens for the first time, it asks you to sign in. You can use a Google account, a GitHub account, or an email address. This account tracks your subscription and usage, and it syncs your settings if you enable that.

The free Hobby tier starts immediately, no credit card required. It includes a monthly allowance of Tab completions and a limited number of AI requests. That is plenty for working through this guide and building your first projects. You can upgrade to Pro later from inside the app or on the website when you start hitting the limits.

One small but important step: after signing in, open Cursor Settings (the gear icon, then Cursor Settings) and look at the Privacy section. Decide now whether you want Privacy Mode on. With it on, Cursor holds zero data retention agreements with its model providers, meaning your code is not stored or used for training. We cover the full privacy picture in a later lesson, but setting your preference early is good hygiene.

## Verify the install

Open the integrated terminal inside Cursor with Ctrl+` (backtick) on any platform, or Cmd+` on macOS, and check that your normal tools are visible:

```
node --version
python3 --version
git --version
```

Cursor uses your system's shells and tools, so if these work in your regular terminal, they work here. If a command is not found, fix your system PATH first, since Cursor inherits it.

Finally, confirm the AI is reachable: press Cmd+L (Ctrl+L) to open the chat panel and ask "are you working?" You should get a reply in a few seconds. If it hangs, check your internet connection and any corporate firewall, since Cursor needs to reach its servers for every AI feature. Offline mode does not exist. That is worth knowing before you board a plane.

lessons.title: Sign in and import your VS Code life
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why migration is painless

The number one fear about switching editors is losing your setup: your theme, your extensions, your carefully tuned keybindings. Cursor was designed to erase that fear. Because it is a fork of VS Code, it speaks the same configuration language, and the import process takes minutes.

## Import in three clicks

During first launch, Cursor offers to import from VS Code automatically. If you skipped that screen, you can do it anytime: open the Command Palette with Cmd+Shift+P (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows and Linux), type "import," and choose the VS Code import option. It brings over:

- Extensions: your linters, formatters, themes, and language packs install automatically
- Settings: font size, tab width, format-on-save, and every other preference
- Keybindings: if you customized shortcuts, they carry over
- Snippets and themes: your colors and code templates come along

After importing, glance through your extensions list and disable anything Cursor replaces natively. You do not need a separate AI assistant extension, for example. Redundant extensions slow startup and can fight over the same shortcuts.

## Sign in to the services that matter

Two sign-ins are worth doing on day one. First, your Cursor account itself, which you did at install. Second, connect your GitHub account if you use GitHub, since Cursor's Git integration and some agent features work more smoothly with it connected. You will find this under Cursor Settings, in the integrations area.

If your team uses Cursor's Business tier, your admin may invite you to an organization. Accepting the invite applies your team's settings, like enforced Privacy Mode and shared model restrictions, automatically.

## Make it yours

Spend ten minutes on comfort settings now and save yourself months of friction:

```
# Open settings with Cmd+, (Ctrl+,) and search for these:
- Font size: pick what your eyes like (14 is a common default)
- Format on save: turn it on, your future self says thanks
- Tab completion: confirm it is enabled under Cursor Settings > Tab
- Theme: import your favorite or try the Cursor defaults
```

One more recommendation: learn exactly three shortcuts today, Cmd+K (Ctrl+K) for inline edit, Cmd+L (Ctrl+L) for chat, and Tab for accepting completions. Everything else can wait. These three are 80 percent of the daily value.

## If the import misses something

Occasionally an extension does not transfer cleanly, usually one that depends on a native binary for your old machine's architecture. If something misbehaves after import, uninstall it inside Cursor and reinstall fresh from the extension marketplace. Your settings for that extension usually survive because they live in your settings file, not in the extension itself.

Also note that Cursor keeps its own settings files separate from VS Code's. Changes you make in Cursor never touch your VS Code installation, so you can run both side by side while you transition. Many developers keep VS Code around for a month as a safety net, then wonder why they ever needed it.

lessons.title: Open your first project and take the tour
lessons.bodyMd:
## Open a folder, any folder

Cursor works on folders, not files. Go to File, then Open Folder, and pick any code project you have. No project handy? Create one:

```
mkdir my-first-cursor-project
cd my-first-cursor-project
cursor .
```

That last command opens the folder in Cursor (the installer adds the `cursor` command to your PATH). If it does not work, you can always use File, then Open Folder from inside the app.

When a folder opens, Cursor starts indexing it in the background. You will see a small status indicator while it builds a searchable map of your code. For a small project this takes seconds. For a large one, a few minutes. Indexing is what powers the @Codebase mention and the Agent's ability to navigate your project, so let it finish before judging the AI's knowledge of your code.

## The five areas of the screen

Take a sixty second tour. You already know most of this from VS Code, but notice where the AI lives:

1. The activity bar on the far left: Explorer, Search, Source Control, and Extensions, just like VS Code. The Cursor chat lives here too, or in the right sidebar depending on your layout.
2. The editor in the center: this is where Tab completion appears as ghost text as you type.
3. The chat panel: press Cmd+L (Ctrl+L) to open it. This is your conversation space with the AI.
4. The terminal at the bottom: Ctrl+` toggles it. The Agent can run commands here with your permission.
5. The status bar at the very bottom: shows your branch, errors, and Cursor-specific items like indexing progress.

## Your first three moves

Do these right now, in order, to feel the whole loop:

First, create a file called `hello.py` and type `def greet(name):` then press Enter. Watch Tab completion suggest the function body. Press Tab to accept it.

Second, select the function, press Cmd+K (Ctrl+K), and type "add a docstring and handle empty names." Watch the selection rewrite itself in place.

Third, press Cmd+L (Ctrl+L) and ask "explain what this function does." The chat answers using the actual code on your screen.

Congratulations. You just used all three core interaction levels: completion, inline edit, and chat. The rest of this guide is about getting good at each one and learning when to reach for which.

## A note on the files you will see

As you explore, you will notice Cursor creates a `.cursor` folder in some projects once you start using rules or MCP servers. You do not need to touch it today. Just know it is where your project's AI configuration will live, and it is worth committing the non-secret parts to git so your whole team shares the same AI behavior. We will build those files by hand in Chapter 4, and by then they will feel familiar instead of mysterious.

One more habit to start now: glance at the status bar whenever the AI seems confused about your project. If indexing is still running or paused, the AI is working with an incomplete map. A thirty second wait for indexing to finish often fixes a confusing answer better than rephrasing your question three times.

lessons.title: Tab completion: your new typing speed
lessons.bodyMd:
## Ghost text that thinks ahead

Tab completion is the feature you will use hundreds of times a day, so it is worth understanding deeply. As you type, Cursor shows suggested code in faint gray text, called ghost text. Press Tab to accept it, Esc to dismiss it, or just keep typing to ignore it. That is the entire interaction, and it becomes muscle memory within a day.

What makes Cursor's version special is prediction depth. Older autocomplete finished the current line. Cursor's custom model predicts multi-line edits: whole functions, the next several lines of a loop, even the next step in a sequence you are building. It also does something called next-edit prediction. After you change one thing, it anticipates the follow-up changes you are about to make, like updating the matching test or the other call site.

## Build the acceptance reflex

The key skill is fast, confident judgment. For each suggestion, you are asking one question: is this what I would have written? Accept with Tab when yes. The suggestions are usually right for boilerplate, standard patterns, and code that follows directly from what is around it.

Dismiss with Esc when the suggestion looks off, and watch for the classic failure modes: hallucinated API methods that do not exist, subtly wrong variable names, and logic that looks plausible but handles edge cases differently than you need. These happen in maybe one suggestion out of five, which is exactly why you never accept blindly on important code.

Two power moves most beginners miss. First, partial accept: press Cmd+Right Arrow (Ctrl+Right Arrow) to accept just the next word of a suggestion instead of the whole thing. This is perfect when the start is right but the ending drifts. Second, if you dismissed something and want it back, keep typing a character or two and it often reappears with a better guess.

## Tune it to your taste

Under Cursor Settings, then Tab, you will find the completion controls. The useful ones:

- Enable or disable Tab completion entirely (some people turn it off for prose or config files)
- Adjust how aggressively it suggests (conservative means fewer, more confident suggestions)
- The model choice for completions, if your plan includes options

A practical tip: Tab completion learns from your recent edits and open files. If suggestions feel irrelevant, open the files related to what you are writing. The model weights open tabs heavily, so giving it the right files to look at is the simplest way to improve accuracy. Context is king, even for autocomplete.

## The honest math

Reviewers who measured carefully found Tab completion alone saving 45 to 60 minutes a day for working developers, with acceptance rates climbing as the model learns your style. But the number that matters is yours. For one week, notice how often you press Tab versus Esc. If you are accepting most suggestions and your code still passes tests, the feature is earning its keep. If you find yourself fixing bad completions often, slow down and read before you Tab. The tool is fast. Your judgment is the quality control.

lessons.title: Cmd+K: inline editing without leaving your flow
lessons.bodyMd:
## The select, describe, done loop

Cmd+K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux) is the fastest way to change code you have already written. The loop is always the same: select the code, press Cmd+K, describe the change in plain English, press Enter, review the diff. The editor shows you exactly what changed, and you accept or revert.

Try it on something real. Select a function and type "convert this to async/await." Select a messy conditional and type "simplify this logic." Select an untyped JavaScript function and type "add TypeScript types." Each of these takes five to ten seconds, and they are the kind of micro-tasks that eat a surprising amount of a developer's day when done by hand.

## What it is for, and what it is not for

Cmd+K shines on small, well-defined transformations of existing code. Renaming a variable across a function. Adding error handling with retries. Converting a callback API to promises. Translating a snippet from one style to another. These are tasks where you know exactly what you want and the change is contained in the selection.

It is the wrong tool for two situations. First, changes that span multiple files, like renaming a function everywhere it is used. That is Agent territory, which we cover next. Second, open-ended design questions like "how should I structure this feature." For those, use the chat panel, where you can have a back-and-forth before committing to code.

A good rule of thumb: if you can describe the change in one sentence and point at the code, use Cmd+K. If you need a paragraph and several files, use the Agent.

## Write good inline instructions

The quality of the result tracks the quality of your one-liner. Compare "fix this" with "handle the case where the user list is empty by returning an empty array instead of throwing." The first invites guessing. The second is a specification.

Three habits that improve results: name the concrete change you want, mention constraints ("keep the existing function signature"), and state the edge cases you care about. You do not need to write essays. One clear sentence beats three vague ones.

## Follow-up edits

Here is the part beginners miss: Cmd+K is conversational. After it applies a change, you can press Cmd+K again on the result and refine: "now also log a warning when the list is empty." This iterative loop, rough change then polish, is often faster than trying to specify perfection in a single prompt. Think of it as sketching with words, then tightening the sketch.

lessons.title: Chat: ask your codebase anything
lessons.bodyMd:
## Your codebase, now conversational

Press Cmd+L (Ctrl+L) and a chat panel opens beside your code. This is where you ask questions, explore unfamiliar code, and request changes that you will review before applying. Unlike a generic chatbot, Cursor's chat already knows your project: the open file, your recent edits, and the indexed codebase are all available as context.

Ask the kinds of questions you would ask a senior teammate. "Where is user authentication handled?" "What does this function do?" "Why is this test failing?" Because the chat can see your actual code, its answers reference real files and line numbers instead of generic advice. Clicking a reference jumps straight to the code, which makes chat a genuinely good way to learn an unfamiliar codebase.

## Point the AI with @-mentions

The chat is smart, but you make it smarter by pointing. Type @ in the chat box and you get a menu of context sources:

- @Files (or @file): attach a specific file, like `@Files src/auth/login.ts`
- @Folders: attach a whole directory
- @Codebase: let the AI search your entire indexed project for relevant code
- @Docs: pull in documentation you have indexed, like framework docs
- @Git: reference your git history, diffs, and recent commits
- @Web: let the AI search the internet for current information

A practical pattern: start broad, then narrow. Ask "how does the checkout flow work" with @Codebase and let it find the relevant files. Then follow up with @Files on the specific file to dig deeper. Broad for discovery, narrow for precision.

## Chat modes: ask, edit, and plan

The chat input has a mode selector, and choosing the right one matters. In Ask mode, the AI answers questions and does not touch your files. Use this when learning or exploring. In Edit mode, it can modify files directly, applying changes you review. Plan mode is for bigger tasks: the AI researches your codebase and writes a step-by-step plan first, and you approve the plan before anything changes.

Beginners should live in Ask mode for the first week. It is the safe sandbox. You get all the explanatory power with zero risk of unwanted edits. Move to Edit and Plan modes once you are comfortable reviewing diffs.

## From chat to code

When the chat suggests code, you will see an Apply button. Clicking it inserts the change into your file as a diff you can review, accept, or revert. This two-step flow, chat proposes, you dispose, is the safety net that makes chat trustworthy. Never apply a change you do not understand. If the explanation is unclear, ask a follow-up: "explain that change line by line." A good AI pair programmer does not mind explaining itself, and neither should you mind asking.

lessons.title: Agent mode: let Cursor do the typing
lessons.bodyMd:
## What the Agent actually does

Agent mode is the biggest leap in Cursor. You describe a goal, and the AI works like a junior developer: it reads files, makes a plan, edits multiple files, runs terminal commands, observes the results, and iterates. Press Cmd+I (Ctrl+I) to open the Composer, or use the Agent option in the chat panel, and type something like "add a password reset flow with email."

What happens next is the magic and the part to watch carefully. The Agent searches your codebase for the relevant pieces, proposes or executes a plan, creates and edits files, runs your tests or build, reads any errors, and fixes them. You watch the whole process unfold in the panel, with each file change shown as a reviewable diff.

## The approval habit

The Agent can run terminal commands, which means it can do real things to your machine. Cursor asks for your approval before running commands by default. Keep it that way while you are learning. When the Agent wants to run `npm install` or execute a test suite, you will see the exact command and can approve or deny it.

This approval step is your safety rail. A useful practice: let the Agent run read-only commands freely (tests, builds, searches) but pause and think before approving anything that writes, deletes, or publishes. The setting that auto-approves everything exists, and experienced users do turn it on for trusted projects, but it is not a beginner setting.

## Give the Agent a good brief

Agent results track brief quality more than anything else. A weak brief: "add auth." A strong brief:

```
Add email/password login to this Next.js app:
- Use the existing Supabase client in lib/supabase.ts
- Create a login page at app/login/page.tsx
- Show clear error messages for wrong passwords
- Do not change the signup flow
```

Notice the pattern: what to build, which existing pieces to reuse, where it goes, and what not to touch. Constraints are as important as goals. The Agent cannot read your mind, but it is excellent at following a clear spec.

## Supervise like a senior engineer

While the Agent works, your job is review. Watch the diffs as they appear. If it goes down a wrong path, stop it, explain what is wrong, and let it correct course. Small corrections early beat big rewrites later.

When it finishes, do your own verification: run the tests, click through the feature, check the edge cases. The Agent is genuinely good, but reviewers consistently find it misses edge cases and occasionally hallucinates APIs. Your sign-off is what makes the output trustworthy.

One more honest note: Agent runs consume AI requests, and on the credit-based pricing those cost more than chat messages. For learning and small tasks, chat and Cmd+K are cheaper. Save the Agent for multi-file work where it earns its keep.

lessons.title: Rules: teach Cursor your conventions once
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why the AI keeps making the same mistakes

You will notice a pattern: the AI writes good code, but not your code. It uses double quotes when your project uses single quotes. It puts components in the wrong folder. It forgets that your team never uses a certain library. You correct it, and next session it does it again. Rules fix this permanently.

Rules are instruction files that Cursor reads automatically and includes in the AI's context. Write your conventions down once, and every future completion, chat answer, and Agent run follows them. It is the highest leverage configuration in the editor.

## The modern way: .cursor/rules

Create a folder called `.cursor/rules` in your project root. Inside it, add markdown files with the `.mdc` extension. Each file has a small frontmatter header that controls when it applies:

```
---
description: TypeScript conventions for all TS files
globs: **/*.ts, **/*.tsx
alwaysApply: false
---

# TypeScript conventions
- Use strict mode, never use `any`
- Prefer interfaces over types for object shapes
- All API responses must be validated with Zod
```

The frontmatter fields mean: `description` tells the Agent what the rule is for, `globs` limits the rule to matching files (so TypeScript rules do not fire when you edit CSS), and `alwaysApply: true` would attach the rule to every single request. Keep `alwaysApply` false unless the rule truly is universal, like "never commit secrets."

You may also see references to a single `.cursorrules` file in the project root. That was the original mechanism and still works, but the `.cursor/rules` directory is the current recommended approach because it lets you organize rules by topic and scope them with globs.

## What makes a good rule

The best rules are short, declarative, and specific. Constraints beat explanations. Compare "please try to write clean code" (useless, the AI already tries) with "API routes must return { data } or { error } shapes, never bare values" (excellent, it prevents a real recurring mistake).

Start with three kinds of rules. First, banned patterns: the things you never want to see, like a deprecated library or an insecure pattern. These have the highest return on investment because they prevent correction loops. Second, architecture rules: where things live and how layers talk to each other. These matter most for Agent mode, since the Agent plans before it writes. Third, style rules: formatting and naming conventions your linter does not already enforce.

Keep each rule file focused on one topic, small enough that a teammate could review it in one sitting. Five sharp rules beat fifty vague ones.

## Rules beyond your project

Cursor also supports User Rules, which apply to everything you do across all projects, set in Cursor Settings. Put personal preferences there ("I prefer functional components", "explain code with brief comments"). And on team plans, admins can set Team Rules that apply to everyone. The precedence runs Team, then Project, then User, so more specific organizational needs win over personal taste.

lessons.title: Codebase indexing: how Cursor learns your project
lessons.bodyMd:
## The map behind the magic

When you open a folder in Cursor, it builds an index of your code in the background: a searchable map of every file, function, and symbol. This index is what lets @Codebase find the right files and what lets the Agent navigate a project it has never seen before. Understanding the index helps you keep it fast and accurate.

Here is the honest version of how it works. Cursor computes vector embeddings of your files, which are numerical summaries of what the code means, not copies of the code itself. Those embeddings and some metadata, like obfuscated file paths, are stored on Cursor's servers so semantic search can run quickly. The actual file text is not stored as-is, and Cursor states the embeddings are not used to train models. If you disable indexing, even those derived artifacts are not created.

## Keep the index healthy

The index is only as good as the project it maps. Three habits keep it useful:

First, use a `.cursorignore` file in your project root. It works like `.gitignore`: list the files and folders the AI should never see. At minimum, exclude secrets and noise:

```
# .cursorignore
.env*
*.pem
*.key
node_modules/
dist/
build/
*.log
```

This keeps sensitive files out of the AI's context and makes searches faster by skipping generated folders.

Second, keep your project structure sane. The index mirrors your organization. A project with clear folders (components, lib, app) gives better search results than a flat pile of fifty files, because the AI uses paths as hints about what code does.

Third, watch the status bar. If indexing is stuck or failing on a huge folder, excluding that folder in `.cursorignore` usually fixes it. Generated code, vendored dependencies, and giant data files do not belong in the index.

## Search strategies that work

With a healthy index, @Codebase becomes your codebase tour guide. Ask discovery questions: "where do we handle payments", "how is state managed in this app", "show me all the API routes." The AI searches semantically, so it finds conceptually related code even when the words do not match exactly.

A useful two-step pattern: ask @Codebase to find, then @Files to focus. The first query discovers which files matter. The second attaches exactly those files for a deep dive. This keeps the AI's context tight and its answers precise, which is the practical application of the golden rule from Chapter 1: enough context to be accurate, not so much that it gets confused.

## When the index is wrong

Sometimes the AI confidently references code that does not exist or describes a file inaccurately. This usually means the index is stale (you changed files faster than it reindexed) or the project is large enough that search returned approximate matches. When an answer looks suspicious, verify by opening the file yourself, then tell the chat what you found. A quick "that file does not exist, the real one is X" teaches the current conversation and gets you back on track.

lessons.title: MCP: plug the outside world into Cursor
Debug with AI: from error message to fix
lessons.bodyMd:
## The fastest debugging loop you have ever used

Debugging used to mean reading a stack trace, guessing, adding print statements, and repeating. With Cursor, the loop compresses: the AI reads the error, finds the relevant code, proposes a fix, and you verify. Here is the workflow that experienced users settle into.

Step one: reproduce the error where the AI can see it. Run your code in Cursor's integrated terminal so the output is right there. When the error appears, select the error text in the terminal, press Cmd+L (Ctrl+L), and ask "why is this failing?" The chat receives both the error and your codebase context, which is usually enough for it to pinpoint the cause.

Step two: let it investigate. In Ask mode, say "trace where this value comes from" or "find where this function is called." The AI follows the trail through your files faster than you can click through them manually. This is where codebase indexing pays for itself.

Step three: apply the fix with Cmd+K or the Agent, then rerun immediately. The tight loop, error to fix to rerun in under a minute, is what makes AI debugging feel magical. But the verification step is non-negotiable. The AI's fix might silence the error while breaking something else. Run your tests.

## Teach it your error patterns

Some errors recur in every project: CORS issues, environment variables that are missing in one context, type mismatches at API boundaries. When you solve one, add it to your rules file. A rule like "API routes must validate environment variables at startup and fail with a clear message" prevents the next occurrence instead of just fixing this one.

You can also paste recurring errors into the chat and ask "what is the systematic fix for this class of error, not just this instance?" The AI is good at generalizing from a specific failure to a pattern, and that pattern becomes a rule.

## When the AI gets stuck

It happens. The AI proposes three fixes and none work. The sign of an experienced user is knowing when to change strategy instead of hammering the same prompt. Try these in order:

First, widen the context. The bug might live in a file the AI has not seen. Attach the suspected files with @Files or run a @Codebase search for related code.

Second, ask for a hypothesis list instead of a fix: "give me the three most likely causes ranked by probability." This forces structured thinking and often surfaces the real cause as option two or three.

Third, rubber-duck it. Explain the problem to the chat in your own words, step by step, including what you expected versus what happened. Half the time, you will spot the bug yourself mid-explanation. The AI makes an excellent duck because it asks clarifying questions.

Fourth, check the boring stuff. Is the dev server running the latest code? Is the environment variable actually set in this terminal? Did you save the file? AI debugging is so fast that it is easy to skip the fundamentals. The fundamentals still cause a large share of all bugs.

lessons.title: Project walkthrough: build a personal dashboard
lessons.bodyMd:
## What we are building

Time to put it all together. In this lesson you will build a small but real project: a personal dashboard web page that shows the time, a todo list that saves to the browser, and a notes area. It is simple enough to finish in one sitting and rich enough to use every Cursor feature: Tab completion for the boilerplate, Cmd+K for refinements, chat for questions, and the Agent for the multi-file structure.

We will use plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single project folder. No frameworks, no build tools. The point is the workflow, not the stack.

## Step 1: scaffold with the Agent

Open a new empty folder in Cursor and press Cmd+I (Ctrl+I) to open the Composer. Give it a clear brief:

```
Create a personal dashboard page:
- index.html with a header showing the current time, updating every second
- A todo list: add items, check them off, delete them, saved in localStorage
- A notes textarea that autosaves to localStorage
- styles.css with a clean, modern dark theme
- app.js with all the logic, organized in small functions
- Everything must work by just opening index.html in a browser
```

Watch the Agent create the three files. Review each diff as it appears. When it finishes, open index.html in your browser and confirm the basics work: the clock ticks, todos save across refreshes, notes persist.

## Step 2: refine with Cmd+K

Now polish like a developer. Open `styles.css`, select the todo list styles, press Cmd+K (Ctrl+K), and type "make completed todos fade to 50 percent opacity with a strikethrough." Select the header in `index.html`, Cmd+K, "add a greeting that changes based on time of day."

Each refinement takes seconds. Notice the rhythm: you decide what good looks like, the AI does the typing, you verify in the browser. This is the specification and verification loop from Chapter 1, running at full speed.

## Step 3: add a feature with chat first

Here is a feature with a design decision in it: todo priorities. Before writing code, press Cmd+L (Ctrl+L) in Ask mode and discuss: "I want to add priority levels to todos. What is the simplest data model, and how should the UI show it?" Talk through the options. Then switch to Edit mode or the Agent and implement the agreed design.

This chat-first pattern is the professional habit. Design in conversation, implement with assistance, verify by running. It prevents the classic AI failure mode of confidently building the wrong thing at high speed.

## Step 4: lock in what you learned

Before closing the project, do two things. First, create `.cursor/rules/dashboard.mdc` with the conventions this project taught you:

```
---
description: Dashboard project conventions
globs: **/*.js
alwaysApply: false
---

# Dashboard conventions
- All state persists to localStorage under keys prefixed with "dash:"
- Functions must be small and single-purpose
- No frameworks, vanilla JS only
```

Second, write down the three moments where the AI saved you the most time and the one moment it led you astray. That list is your personal calibration. Every developer's is different, and knowing yours is what turns a powerful tool into a reliable one.

lessons.title: Privacy and pricing: what to know before you commit
lessons.bodyMd:
## Where your code actually goes

Every AI feature in Cursor sends some of your code to servers for processing. That is not a scandal, it is how the product works. But you should understand the flow so you can make informed choices.

Three destinations matter. Tab completions go to Cursor's own model servers. Chat and Agent requests go to the model provider you selected, such as OpenAI or Anthropic, under Cursor's agreements with them. Codebase indexing computes vector embeddings of your files, numerical summaries, not copies, which are stored on Cursor's infrastructure for fast semantic search. The raw file text is not stored as-is for indexing.

Cursor is SOC 2 certified, which means an independent auditor verified its security controls. It also maintains zero data retention agreements with its model providers: with the right settings, your code is not stored by providers and not used to train models.

## Privacy Mode and .cursorignore

The main control is Privacy Mode, found in Cursor Settings under General. Turn it on and Cursor enforces zero retention with providers and keeps telemetry anonymous. On Business plans, admins can enforce it for the whole team, and members cannot turn it off individually.

The second control is `.cursorignore`, which excludes files from indexing and AI context entirely. Use it for secrets and noise:

```
# .cursorignore
.env*
*.pem
*.key
credentials.json
node_modules/
```

One caution from security reviewers: Cursor's data sharing setting has historically defaulted to on, allowing product improvement use of your data. Check Settings, then Privacy, and turn off anything you are not comfortable with. Defaults deserve a look, not blind trust. And on any plan, never paste production secrets into chat. The AI does not need your real API keys to help you write code that uses them.

## The pricing tiers, honestly

Cursor's plans, as of 2026: Hobby is free and includes a monthly allowance of completions plus a limited number of AI requests, enough for learning and light side projects. Pro is 20 dollars a month with a much larger allowance and access to frontier models. Pro+ at 60 dollars a month triples the allowance for heavy users. Business is 40 dollars per user per month with admin controls, SSO, and enforced privacy. Ultra at 200 dollars a month is for teams with extreme usage.

The honest complication: since 2025, usage above the included allowance runs on credits, and different models cost different amounts. Heavy users report real monthly costs of 30 to 50 dollars on the 20 dollar plan because they buy extra credits during intense weeks. When you hit the limit, Cursor does not stop working, it falls back to slower models, and the quality drop is noticeable.

## Choosing your tier

Start on Hobby. It is free and sufficient for everything in this guide. Move to Pro when you hit the request limit in normal use, which for a daily builder usually happens within the first month or two. Watch your usage dashboard for a month before considering Pro+. And if you are choosing for a team, price the Business tier against your compliance needs: enforced Privacy Mode and audit logs are the real reasons teams pay more, not just the extra requests.

lessons.title: Best practices and where to go next
lessons.bodyMd:
## The ten habits of effective Cursor users

Everything in this guide distills to habits. Here are the ten that separate developers who thrive with Cursor from those who fight it:

1. Review every diff. The AI writes the code, you own the code. No exceptions.
2. Be specific in prompts. One clear sentence beats three vague ones.
3. Give context deliberately. Attach the right files, write rules, keep the index healthy.
4. Design before implementing. Use Ask mode to think, Edit mode to build.
5. Start small with the Agent. One feature at a time, verify between steps.
6. Keep approvals on for terminal commands until you trust the project setup.
7. Write rules for recurring mistakes. Every correction you repeat is a rule you have not written yet.
8. Run the tests. AI-generated code needs verification like any code.
9. Learn the code it writes. Ask "explain this" for anything you could not write yourself.
10. Keep secrets out. Use .cursorignore, never paste real credentials into chat.

## Staying sharp as the tool evolves

Cursor ships fast. Features arrive monthly, shortcuts shift, pricing evolves. The way to stay current without drowning: skim the official changelog when you update, follow one or two practitioners whose workflow posts you trust, and revisit your rules files quarterly. Rules written for last year's Cursor sometimes fight this year's features.

More importantly, keep building your fundamentals. The developers who get the most from AI editors are the ones who could do the work without them, just slower. Data structures, how the web works, debugging discipline, system design: these compound, while any specific tool's tricks depreciate. Use the time Cursor saves you to learn the deeper things, not to ship more shallow things.

## Your next three moves

First, build one real project with Cursor this week, something you actually want to exist. Tutorials teach features. Projects teach judgment.

Second, write your first rules file for that project. Start with three rules: one banned pattern, one architecture convention, one style preference. Feel it working across sessions.

Third, connect one MCP server for a service you use, GitHub or your database. Extending the Agent's reach is the skill that separates casual users from power users.

## The bigger picture

Cursor is one point on a larger trend: software development is becoming a conversation. You describe intent, the machine handles implementation, and your judgment moves up the stack. The developers thriving in this shift are not the fastest typists. They are the clearest thinkers, the most careful reviewers, and the most disciplined verifiers.

You now have the complete toolkit: setup, daily workflow, power features, and the habits that make it all trustworthy. The editor is ready. The rest is building.
